chapters.file: ch18 - The Cost of the Code Ethical Consequences in High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident.md
chapters.relation: Ken Hada reads High Noon and The Ox-Bow Incident through Nussbaum's neo-Aristotelian critique of Kantian duty. Will Kane's absolute, self-sacrificing return to face Frank Miller and Major Tetley's honor-bound insistence on hanging the accused both exemplify the Kantian categorical imperative applied without regard to consequences. The essay argues that the films themselves undermine this code: Kane's triumph brings no joy and Tetley's rigid 'reason' masks self-interest and produces the lynching of three innocent men. Following Nussbaum, it holds that attention to particulars, emotion, and social context—embodied by Davies in Ox-Bow—yields more just moral perception than blind allegiance to an absolute rule.

chapters.file: ch19 - “Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch.md
chapters.relation: Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.

chapters.file: ch20 - No Country for Old Men The Decline of Ethics and the West(ern).md
chapters.relation: William J. Devlin argues that No Country for Old Men deconstructs the western's three ingredients (moral hero, comprehensible villain, redemptive showdown) and collapses the genre into Nietzschean nihilism. Where Shane's courage is legible through Aristotelian virtue-ethics and Kantian deontology, Sheriff Bell grows old and afraid, walking away rather than confronting evil. Anton Chigurh perverts deontology—killing on 'principle' and because he 'gave his word'—while his coin flips invoke Nagel's moral luck to disclaim responsibility, so the good/bad polarity dissolves and, as Ellis says, 'you can't stop what's comin'.'

chapters.file: ch21 - The Northwestern McCabe and Mrs. Miller.md
chapters.relation: Deborah Knight and George McKnight read Altman's McCabe and Mrs. Miller as an 'end-of-genre' western in the ironic mode, using Frye's Aristotle-derived mythos to map the classic western's binary oppositions (hero/villain, community/wilderness, virgin/whore) and then show the film collapsing them. Against Nussbaum's and Booth's ethical criticism, which extols works that make us 'finely aware and richly responsible,' they argue irony is itself a moral stance of detached scrutiny: McCabe is no hero but a vulgar, unimaginative businessman crushed by the Harrison Shaughnessy company and shot in the back in the snow while the town obliviously saves its burning church, dramatizing the implosion of the western's moral vision.

chapters.file: ch22 - Part 4 On the Fringe The Encounter with the Other.md
ch23 - Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western.md
chapters.relation: Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.

chapters.file: ch24 - Regeneration through Stories and Song The View from the Other Side of the West in Smoke Signals.md
chapters.relation: Richard Gilmore reads Smoke Signals—the first feature written, directed, and coproduced by Native Americans—against Slotkin's myth of regeneration through violence, arguing it offers regeneration through stories and song instead. Drawing on Wilshire's claim that pragmatism is 'aboriginal,' he links Emerson and Thoreau's transcendentalism and Peirce's 'law of mind' to Deloria's American Indian metaphysics and Hyde's gift economy: Arlene's fry-bread story and Thomas's storytelling repair broken relationships, and Victor's final act of forgiving his father (and withholding that Arnold caused the fatal fire) is read as the film's central gift, completing relationships that violence had severed.

chapters.file: ch25 - Go West, Young Woman! Hegel's Dialectic and Women's Identities in Western Films.md
chapters.relation: Gary Heba and Robin Murphy map women's identities in westerns onto Hegel's three-stage dialectic (aufheben as maintain/negate/transform), grafting on Bakhtin's monoglossic/heteroglossic discourse and Mulvey's and de Beauvoir's feminist film theory. Settler women (Marian in Shane, the mothers of The Searchers) are monoglossic—silenced, family-bound bearers of meaning; town women (Mrs. French in Appaloosa, Lily in How the West Was Won) are heteroglossic, sexualized spectacles marked by costume; and post-1970s figures like Ellen in The Quick and the Dead and Sara in Two Mules for Sister Sara become 'x-glossic,' transformational identities that subvert the male-gaze code and exceed the settler/town binary.

chapters.file: ch26 - Beating a Live Horse The Elevation and Degradation of Horses in Westerns.md
chapters.relation: Jennifer L. McMahon gives an existential account of Americans' ambivalence toward horses in westerns: because horses mirror human anxiety, herd-boundness, and the flight instinct that Sartre and Heidegger locate at the core of being, we transfer our self-loathing onto them and, driven by Nietzsche's will to power and Hegel's lord-and-bondsman struggle for recognition, we break them to prove our own mastery. Reading breaking scenes in All the Pretty Horses and The Horse Whisperer via Foucault's Discipline and Punish (the round pen as panopticon producing 'docile bodies'), she contrasts films like Hidalgo and The Electric Horseman that model Hegelian reciprocity, urging us to 'let go, turn in, and hook on' rather than dominate.

holes.name: Tzvetan Todorov
holes.what: A structuralist literary theorist and philosopher whose The Conquest of America analyzes the self's encounter with the cultural Other, criticizing both the assimilation of difference and its translation into hierarchy.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire analytic frame is Todorov's typology of alterity (equality vs. difference, Columbus, Las Casas, Sepulveda), and no taxonomy philosopher supplies this theory of the Other.

holes.name: Alterity and the Encounter with the Other
holes.what: The problem of representing the cultural Other as simultaneously equal and different, rather than either assimilating it to the self or ranking it as inferior.
holes.why: The chapter argues that western films' Native Americans are egocentric projections that fail Todorov's demand to grant the Other both equality and difference; the taxonomy's 'levinas-face' concerns ethical obligation, not this representational politics of alterity.
